facts: Practice Guide 40 is organised as six plan supplements covering mapping basis, plan preparation, boundaries, determined boundaries, title plans and other plan services.
The collection brings together HM Land Registry guidance specifically relating to plans.
HM Land Registry states that it provides factual information and impartial procedural advice.
Ordnance Survey mapping shows surveyed topographic features and is not intended to represent property boundaries.
HM Land Registry uses OS MasterMap as the basis for its plans.
The guide identifies typical title-plan scales of 1:1250 for urban land, 1:2500 for rural land and 1:10000 for mountain or moorland.
Deed plans are an essential element of buying and selling land.
A title plan and register cannot describe land more accurately than the pre-registration deeds allow.
A search plan must show precise extent, stated scale, north point and sufficient surrounding detail, and must not be marked for identification only.
Practice Guide 40 supplement 3 was updated on 1 June 2026.
The guide distinguishes the invisible legal boundary from visible physical boundary features.
General boundaries have no standard tolerance, measurement or ratio connecting title-plan lines to the legal boundary.
A determined boundary records the exact line of a registered estate boundary.
The registrar must be satisfied that the exact line is identified, an arguable case exists and adjoining owners can be identified and notified.
A determined-boundary plan should identify start, end and turning points, show orientation and surrounding detail, and preferably use a scale no smaller than 1:200.
Practice Guide 40 supplement 5 was updated on 13 July 2026.
A registered title comprises the register, the title plan and documents referred to in the register and filed at HM Land Registry.
The title plan must be viewed together with the register.
Supplement 6 describes other plan-related services and mapping guidance.
The guide identifies searches of the index map and Electronic Extent Data as plan-related services.
The guide lists six developing-estate supplements under Practice Guide 41.
Practice Guide 10 was updated on 20 July 2026.
The computerised index map covers land in registered titles and pending first-registration applications.
Accepted spatial polygons must use supported GIS formats and OSGB 1936 British National Grid.

Listing an asset of community value is also a Local Land Charge.

Air Quality Management Areas are considered in plan-making and development-management decisions.

The 1 metre DTM covers approximately 99 percent of England.
It is produced from last or only returns with surface objects removed to model the terrain surface.
The 2022 composite combines the time-stamped archive and National LIDAR Programme surveys.
The 2 metre DTM covers approximately 99 percent of England.
Where repeat surveys exist, the newest best-resolution data is selected.
Resampled data is processed with bilinear interpolation before merging.
The 10 metre DTM covers approximately 99 percent of England.
It is resampled from the 2 metre DTM.
The 10 metre product uses bilinear interpolation.
The time-stamped DSM is an archive of Environment Agency raster elevation surveys dating from 1998.
Available resolutions include 25 centimetres, 50 centimetres, 1 metre and 2 metres.
It is supplied as GeoTIFF rasters in 5 kilometre zips, aligned to the OS Grid and referenced to Ordnance Survey Newlyn.
The National LIDAR Programme provides 1 metre elevation coverage for all England.
Phase-one capture divided England into 302 survey blocks.
Programme products include terrain, surface, first-return, intensity and point-cloud data.
The documented elevation coverage endpoints use OGC WCS 2.0.1.
WCS is the documented service for requesting raw elevation pixels.
The updated service URLs are intended to remain persistent for future dataset updates.
OS Terrain 50 is an open height dataset covering Great Britain.
The product is updated annually in July.
Grid and contour products use common source data and are supplied in 10 kilometre tiles.
OS Terrain 50 is the lower-resolution OS terrain product for landscape visualisation and large-area analysis.
The grid has regular 50 metre post spacing.
The contour product uses 10 metre interval standard contours and includes water boundaries and spot heights.
Grid supply uses ASCII and GML; contour supply includes shapefile, GML, GeoPackage and MBTiles.
Online download is available without registration.
The tiled national supply contains 2,858 tiles arranged in 55 folders.
Grid heights are calculated at pixel centres.
Tiles have no overlapping cells or shared edge values.
Mean high and low water lines are used as heighted breaklines, with average values determined per tile.
ASCII grid heights are supplied alongside GML metadata containing location, spacing and vertical-reference information.
Each 10 kilometre tile has 200 pixels per row at 50 metre spacing.
The ASCII grid origin is at the north-west corner and rows run west to east, moving southward.
Contour layers are supplied in GML 3.2.1.
Each contour tile includes a metadata XML file containing information such as flying date.
Spot heights are automatically selected from the highest mass point within closed contours and z values are rounded to whole metres.
